The post AI and the humanities: crisis or opportunity? appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Scarlett Keating, a Year 12 student who recently completed work experience at HEPI.

In 1965, Cambridge History professor JH Plumb’s edit of ‘The crisis in humanities’ was published, citing the struggle of the humanities to stay relevant in a world of rapid technological and scientific growth. While Plumb was incorrect to imply a collapse of humanities study, he rightly highlighted the need for academic humanists to adapt to a tech-driven world.

Today, the humanities face a similar crisis: the expansion of Large Language Model (LLM) use poses a potential threat to the value of human critical thinking and understanding, while a blog by LSE by Marvin Starominski-Uehara highlights a further risk: devaluing university degrees. If students are submitting AI-generated work, and professors are unable to recognise it as AI (one recent study states that, across eight universities, professors correctly identified AI papers only 53% of the time), then students will graduate without all the skills supposedly gained from their degree. Upon entering employment, this gap will be revealed, which risks discrediting qualifications for all graduates, not just those who (mis)used AI.

AI can serve useful purposes in the study of the humanities which do not impede human skills: generating basic summaries, translating collections of historical text, and managing bibliographies are all practical uses of AI as an assistive tool. However, understanding, argument building, and interpretation of ethics (all areas where AI falls short of human capabilities) should not be short circuited.

While the HEPI / Kortext Student Generative AI Survey found only 12% of respondents placed AI-generated text directly in their assessed work (and a further 25% used edited AI generated text), even this could represent a sufficiently large proportion of students to cause reputational harm for all. However, this issue may also provide the solution to the humanities’ perceived growing irrelevance: graduates who have not supplemented their learning with AI may now present even more value to employers.

So, is there a crisis in humanities, or does the crisis make a humanities degree even more important?

The growth of AI presents a challenge to higher education institutions. They need to guide students to enhance their uniquely human understanding of ideas and ethics. If some people are graduating without the skills certified by their qualification due to misuse of AI, this provides an opportunity for students who have developed inherently human skills through their studies. While AI can diminish the abilities of those who use it excessively and improperly, genuine and interested humanities students face limited competition from AI. This is particularly the case when it comes to the interpretation of ideas, empathy and ethics and the ability to understand ideas alongside cultural nuances and temporal context – largely due to the lack of development in these areas of AI function. This creates a significant disparity between the quality of graduates, making those who truly have the expertise AI lacks stronger candidates for employers and further study opportunities.

Study of the humanities allows students to excel in the areas where AI is lacking for a number of reasons. The humanities nurture an understanding of ethics and the ability to evaluate moral consequences; the ability to think critically by judging the credibility of sources and arguments; and developing an understanding of human behaviours and contexts which can be applied to judgements, while subjects which champion the use of data and calculations may struggle to hold an advantage over AI.

In part, the responsibility for finding the right skills lies with employers, who should ensure their application processes are set up to root out applicants who have graduated with gaps in their capabilities: writing tasks, source interpretation or live problem solving, for example, test authentic human skills. However, it is also vital that universities work to ensure their graduates have high levels of ability in areas where humans excel beyond the scope of AI replication.

There is a head of steam behind the idea that we need assessment methods that better assess human judgement and thinking, as recent pieces from both the University of Manchester and HEPI shows. These include assessments where it is impossible to rely entirely on AI – such as oral exams or asking people to apply what they know to applications to real-world problems. Not only would this prevent the abuse of AI in assessments and coursework, but it would ensure that all students are stretched and taught in ways which speak to their human aspects. This will produce graduates better adapted to a world of AI, and better equipped to surpass competition for jobs and research.

On top of this, in a world dominated by artificial intelligence and technological advancements, it is more important than ever to safeguard the uniquely human qualities which define the humanities. Institutions which have long served as havens for the research and study of the humanities must strive to protect these subjects, and their graduates, from irrelevance.

title: Beyond Access
summary:
Beyond Access quintina.barne… Thu, 10/22/2026 - 03:00 AM Improving credit mobility to advance student success in prison education programs. Byline(s) Sarah Kuczynski Zeia Fawaz Quinn Barton Beyond Access
quintina.barne… Thu, 10/22/2026 - 03:00 AM

Improving credit mobility to advance student success in prison education programs.

Byline(s)
Sarah Kuczynski
Zeia Fawaz
Quinn Barton
full_text:
Transfer remains all too difficult for the average student to navigate. Still, those who learn within carceral facilities can face a unique set of additional challenges when it comes to getting their earned credits to apply to a meaningful credential. As was recently outlined in a June 2026 Inside Higher Ed column, there are complex operational challenges that make it difficult for incarcerated and formerly incarcerated learners and academic record keepers like registrars alike.

Such challenges are compounded by the way curriculum has historically been developed for higher education–in–prison programs, the way collaboration across programs has often been stymied by the necessity for program leaders to compete for resources such as funding and facility access, and the way a student’s access to postsecondary programming tends to depend upon their assignment to a particular correctional facility. The lack of continuity of program provision at women’s facilities can often make it even more challenging for learners to earn postsecondary credentials.

Without greater coordination across programs and institutions, incarcerated students may accumulate substantial college credit without a clear route toward a credential. At a recent graduation for one of the grantees profiled in this piece, an associate degree graduate illustrated the challenge: After years of taking courses from multiple colleges and before entering the grantee’s coordinated degree pathway, she joked that she “probably had enough credits for a Ph.D. at this point.”

The lack of continuity of program provision at women’s facilities can often make the problem even more challenging for learners to earn postsecondary credentials.”

The July 2023 reinstatement of Pell Grants for incarcerated learners has presented the higher education–in–prison field with an opportunity to intentionally build out and refine programming to improve credit mobility for currently and formerly incarcerated learners in exciting ways, as detailed in a 2024 Inside Higher Ed column. Federal regulations governing prison education programs (PEPs) require a minimum standard of transferability to at least one other institution in the state. At the same time, the reinvestment of federal financial aid has encouraged more institutions to enter the space and prompted existing programs to be more intentional about curriculum, given students’ limited Pell eligibility and the short window they often have to complete credentials while incarcerated.

Supporting Credit Mobility for Incarcerated Learners

In its second round of Accelerator Grant funding, the New England Board of Higher Education is supporting institutions seeking to improve or construct credit-mobility pathways that advance student success in PEPs. This work is part of NEBHE’s New England Prison Education Collaborative, a five-year, grant-funded initiative supported by Ascendium Education Group to implement the recommendations from the 2023 New England Commission on the Future of Higher Education in Prison. This initiative works to engage a diverse array of regional stakeholders through state strategic planning, workshops and subgrants.

The request for proposals was released on April 30 and was open to postsecondary institutions in all six New England states with an approved PEP program. Four institutions—one in Connecticut, two in Massachusetts and one in New Hampshire—were each awarded one-year, $100,000 grants to support a credit mobility–focused project. As part of their application, the four recipients detailed actionable project plans and submitted documentation of correctional leadership support. The grantees operate in different carceral contexts that influence their approach to tackling the credit-mobility challenges facing the students they serve.

In Connecticut, Connecticut State Community College, in partnership with Wesleyan University, will strengthen coordination across their complementary offerings, creating clearer pathways from certificate to associate and bachelor’s degree completion. Building on CT State and Wesleyan’s decades-long partnership at the York Correctional Institution, the project will expand coordinated advising, increase access to laptops and academic research materials, and strengthen credit mobility and reverse-transfer opportunities so students can meaningfully apply credit from coursework completed across participating programs.

Through its Future of Work Institute, Massasoit Community College in Massachusetts will use its Accelerator Grant funds to create a 2+2 transfer pathway with Bridgewater State University at Old Colony Correctional Center, expanding access to bachelor’s degree pathways for incarcerated students in the commonwealth. The initiative will align curriculum, streamline credit transfer and provide coordinated advising to support seamless transition from Massasoit’s liberal arts studies associate degree to workforce-aligned bachelor’s programs in fields accessible to those with a criminal record.

Middlesex Community College will offer the community leadership certificate—a credential with a work-based learning component—to students at Middlesex House of Correction. As with their entrepreneurship certificate, this credential will be delivered on-site at MHoC and earned directly as MCC coursework. The work-based learning component will be developed with UTEC in Lowell, Mass., and adapted for correctional settings.

Building on UTEC’s existing on-site presence at MHoC, students will fulfill this component while still incarcerated, co-facilitating support groups or serving as peer mentors under UTEC supervision, removing one of the most significant barriers justice-impacted students face: completing work-based learning while confined. MCC will also train staff and faculty on transcript evaluation and credit for prior learning practices, ensuring consistent evaluation of coursework and helping students carry momentum from certificate completion into degree-seeking status.

In New Hampshire, White Mountains Community College will establish two new 2+2 transfer pathways with the University of New Hampshire at Northern New Hampshire Correctional Facility. The pathways will enable students to transition from WMCC programs into bachelor’s degrees in business management and human services at UNH. This will be the first opportunity for incarcerated individuals to access baccalaureate-level programming in facilities in New Hampshire.

Advancing Research on Credit Mobility

While the Accelerator Grant projects work to improve educational pathways for learners in these three states, the NEPEC team at NEBHE has also launched a first-in-the-nation qualitative research study to better understand the specific experiences of credit transfer for formerly incarcerated learners in New England. Through a survey and series of interviews of formerly incarcerated students and a select number of New England–based experts on credit mobility, the study aims to illuminate ways to improve credit mobility for currently and formerly incarcerated learners in New England and, hopefully, nationwide. The white paper is expected to be released in the spring of 2027.

title: The real reasons there are so few young politicians in the US
summary: No country for young men and women: why do older politicians seem to have such a tight grip on the US political system?
full_text:
Not many US politicians have endured for as long as Hal Rogers, who will go into November's midterm elections seeking his 24th term in the House of Representatives.

The 88-year-old Republican has represented Kentucky's 5th congressional district since 1981, making him the longest serving member of the House of Representatives. He was elected on the same night Ronald Reagan won his first presidential term under the slogan "Let's make America great again", a phrase later revived by Donald Trump.

Among the challengers Rogers beat to win the nomination this year was one 60 years his junior. But Rogers, born in the 1930s, is far from the only senior US politician to have stuck at the job into their 80s.

Others to have done so include US President Donald Trump, 80; Trump's predecessor Joe Biden, who left office at 82; and Nancy Pelosi, who stepped down as the Democratic leader in the House at the same age. Chuck Grassley, 93, is still a senator. He entered politics in 1958, before Alaska and Hawaii were even US states.

The age and health of some politicians has raised widespread concern within both Republican and Democratic circles, however, reigniting questions about whether age limits or health checks should be imposed.

The US is well known for its "gerontocracy", a government ruled by people who are significantly older than most of the adult population.

At the other end of the age spectrum, the US has one of the lowest proportions of lawmakers under the age of 45 among comparable democracies, according to research from the Inter-Parliamentary Union.

So why are so few young people becoming politicians? And for those who do enter politics, can they make a success of it?

Twenty-seven-year-old Republican Riley Owen is one of the few candidates from Gen Z - aged in their early teens to late 20s - from either party running for Congress on 3 November.

Owen is running in a newly created district in Utah that experts say may lean towards the Democrats. He has championed issues including paid maternity leave, restrictions on congressional stock trading and environmental action - all issues that may appeal to Democratic supporters.

When he was confirmed as his party's candidate in the state's 1st congressional district, he walked on stage to Billy Joel's We Didn't Start the Fire, and argued that his generation needed to help renew the American Dream.

The gerontocracy is "a bipartisan issue", he says. "We've got people who have become career politicians, and they spend their lives in Congress." He says this is indicative of a system that is not delivering for Americans.

Owen says the big challenge he faces is the fact that money really talks in US politics. Research suggests campaign donors tend to prefer incumbent candidates.

Indeed, the campaign of his rival Ben McAdams - a 51-year-old Democrat who has previously served in Congress - has so far raised much more cash than Owen's. By mid-October, McAdams had raised over $2.6m (£1.9m), compared with $150,000 raised by Owen, according to records on the Federal Election Commission website.

Owen argues that his generation is uniquely well-placed to understand contemporary political issues, such as the challenges posed by tech. He also disputes any suggestion that a younger candidate necessarily lacks relevant experience - pointing to his own background as a military officer and a White House policy analyst. "I think in politics, just like in industry, we need what's called disruptive innovation," he says.

The age of America's top politicians has long been a talking point. In 1984 Reagan - who was then America's oldest president at age 73 - deflected scrutiny with a quip about the "youth and inexperience" of his opponent Walter Mondale, who was a sprightly 56.

In the US, individual states also have their own legislatures, with a Senate and a House, where many politicians make their start. Many current members of Congress spent years in state politics before running for a seat in Washington.

But the median age of Congress members has ticked upwards over time. Congressional records show that the lowest median ages in the House and Senate were both recorded in the early 1980s - at 48 and 52 respectively.

The average ages of a House member and a senator at the start of the current Congress were 58 and 65 respectively, according to analysis by the Pew Research Center. The median age of a US citizen is 39.

There is now also a sharper focus on the health and acuity of some of the nation's oldest politicians. Joe Biden's age became a major issue while he was in office. To a lesser extent Trump has faced questions too.

So too has Republican Senator Mitch McConnell, 84, with increasing regularity, after a months-long absence from Congress to undergo medical treatment. Meanwhile, on the Democratic side, Maxine Waters, 88, faces a leadership challenge as the lead Democrat on the powerful House Financial Services Committee, with her age considered by some to be a factor counting against her.

Some of the most vocal critics of this so-called gerontocracy have been candidates who identify as democratic socialists, meaning that their political views are further to the left than those of the Democratic Party mainstream. These candidates tend to campaign heavily on the cost of living and other issues that cut through to Millennials and Gen Z, and their supporters skew younger too.

The demographic profile of people who vote tends to skew older, like the elected officials themselves. Pew research highlights that the proportion of non-voters who are young (aged 18 to 29) has been increasing. In the 2020 US election, 25% of non-voters belonged to that age category, according to Pew. Four years later, it had risen to 30%.

Pew adds that voters under 30 were underrepresented in 2024. Voters in that age category made up 20% of the voting-eligible population, though accounted for only 15% of all the votes that were actually cast.

Campaigners argue that these demographic trends matter because they leave some issues underrepresented.

"Yes, that might result in older people being elected, but I think it really skews, too, what issues are important; what issues politicians are incentivised to talk about and to take care of," says Grace Mausser, the co-chair of the New York City wing of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Mausser campaigned for Zohran Mamdani in his winning bid last year to become, at age 34, New York City's youngest mayor since 1892. Mamdani was held up as an example of a rare youthful success story, but his ally Mausser is less concerned with a politician's age than with their outlook.

Mausser says it is not necessarily a problem if someone has been in politics for a long time. Rather, the problem can be what may result from that: "You become so used to the language and the ideas of the political establishment that anything else - any new ideas, whether they come from young people or old people - seem crazy."

She invokes left-wing Democratic senator Bernie Sanders, 85, as an example of an older politician with a long tenure on Capitol Hill who has embraced change and had ideas that have resonated across generations.

In the US, older people hold politicians in far higher esteem than younger people - even more so than in many other countries, according to a Pew survey from spring 2025. Some 62% of 18-34-year-olds were likely to say few or none of their elected officials are honest, compared with 45% of people aged over 50. Of the 25 countries surveyed by Pew, only Greece's young adults had a more pessimistic view of the honesty of politicians.

For one expert who studies political engagement on both sides of the Atlantic, disaffection among young people helps to explain their unwillingness to participate in politics. The issue is not helped by the fact Congress has minimum age requirements for members, he says. Candidates must be 30 to serve as a senator, and 25 to be a representative.

"The one leads to another," remarks James Sloam from Royal Holloway, University of London. "If you don't have enough young people engaged in politics generally, then they won't become representatives."

What is more, Sloam says, young people in the US and the UK alike are alert to the fact that power does not just lie in politics. They are aware there are many other areas of work in which they can wield influence - including over elected officials.

For those young people who do end up in high-profile political positions, the next question is whether they can make a success of it, especially when it comes to parenthood. Over the summer, the stories of two high-profile young women working in Washington raised fresh questions around compatibility of the job with motherhood.

Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, 37, a Democratic congresswoman who took office aged 29, announced that she had started the process of freezing her eggs.

Later the same week in August, Karoline Leavitt, 29, who was appointed the youngest ever White House press secretary almost two years earlier, said she would leave the Trump administration to spend more time with her family, including her newborn baby. She explained: "I cannot be the best mom my two young children deserve while devoting the constant time, energy and attention required of [being] the White House press secretary."

Only a handful of women have given birth while elected to Congress, while a few dozen lawmakers are mothers to children under the age of 18. The federal government, like many US employers, does not offer paid parental leave.

JD Vance, 42, one of the youngest vice-presidents in US history, recently acknowledged that having young children might impact on his own decision to run for the White House in 2028, saying: "We've got four little kids."

America's two-party system is cited as another barrier to young people getting involved with politics.

Sloam, the London academic, says this is because only a relatively narrow range of views are represented. He highlights research that indicates young people are more energised by social movements or issue-based campaigns than by party politics.

And within party politics, he notes the example of Mamdani and others on the political left who appear to be galvanising youth support outside the Democratic Party mainstream. But he cautions that "it's a little bit sporadic at the moment".

The Republican Party has been through its own splintering over the last decade with the advent of Trump's MAGA movement, which appealed to a swathe of young men in the 2024 presidential election.

Some European democracies show a more pluralistic political environment can increase youth engagement, Sloam says. Scandinavian countries, for example, which are more likely to be multi-party, provide a clear counter example because the parties of government in those countries "work with those social movements to try and bring them into the political systems". Citing countries such as Norway, Sloam suggests there is a cycle whereby stronger youth turnout and youth trust in the political system leads to more involvement in politics.

Owen, the Republican, fancies his chances in Utah, despite his opponent's much larger war chest.

Discussing what energises him as a Gen Z candidate, he identifies issues including the role of tech in public life, immigration and cost-of-living concerns. "I'm on the front end of starting my own family and looking at the costs and [asking] how am I going to make it work?" he says.

Asked if he sees any similarities between his campaign and the campaigns of young political candidates on the opposite side of the political spectrum, he says: "I'd break down the 'us versus them' framework, and maybe discard that a little bit… [there is] a bipartisan message that a lot of Americans on both sides of the aisle are feeling: that Washington isn't working for them."

He takes a similar view to Mausser, the democratic socialist in New York, that voters should not necessarily pick a candidate because they are young: what matters is their ideas.

"For me, it's much more about what you support, what you're who you're fighting for, than what year you were born," she says.

title: Workforce Pell Grants give students new options for job training
summary: For decades, federal Pell Grants have helped millions of students from low- and middle-income families afford college. Now, for the first time, that financial aid will also be available for short-term vocational training programs designed to help students enter the workforce. Stephanie Sy reports on the rollout of Workforce Pell for our series, Rethinking College.
full_text:
Geoff Bennett:

For decades, federal Pell Grants have helped millions of students from low- and middle-income families afford college. Now, for the first time, that financial aid will also be available for short-term vocational training programs designed to help students enter the work force.

Stephanie Sy reports on the rollout of Workforce Pell, the largest expansion of the federal grant program in 50 years.

It's part of our higher education series called Rethinking College.

Stephanie Sy:

At Ivy Tech Community College campus in Anderson, Indiana, learning is hands-on.

Woman:

Fourth intercostal space, we're going to put that right here.

Stephanie Sy:

From putting on an EKG to administering shots...

Woman:

Good job. Good technique.

Stephanie Sy:

... to drawing blood. In just eight weeks, these students are trained to become certified clinical medical assistants, or CCMAs. They're the folks at the doctor's office who might take your vital science or get your medical history at the start of your appointment. And they're in high demand, says program chair Sara Standlee.

Sara Standlee, Ivy Tech Community College:

A lot of my students, they'll get hired before they graduate. That's how much of a need there is for medical assistants out there right now, because the fact of the matter is, is we have got a lot of people that need medical care, and we don't have enough people to be able to care for them.

Stephanie Sy:

Twenty-two-year-old Makaila Collins sees becoming a CCMA as a stepping-stone on the way to becoming a registered nurse.

Makaila Collins, Student, Ivy Tech Community College:

I decided to take the route of getting my CCMA first. And then a lot of the times, if you go work for like a big hospital network, they will actually pay for you to go back to nursing school.

Stephanie Sy:

Just getting here took perseverance and waiting a lot of tables.

Makaila Collins:

I had to take a break for a few years and just work just to build up that savings to be able to pay for this class.

Stephanie Sy:

How much was that? Do you remember?

Makaila Collins:

One thousand four hundred and fifty-three dollars.

(LAUGHTER)

Makaila Collins:

I remember exactly because I had to take it all out and then send in the payment.

Stephanie Sy:

But, soon, students in this course will have access to new financial support. This summer, Ivy Tech's certified clinical medical assistant program became the second in the country to be approved for a new federal grant called Workforce Pell.

(CHEERING)

Stephanie Sy:

President Trump signed it into law in the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill.

Nicholas Kent, U.S. Undersecretary of Education: We're actually building the new program to align with industry needs and provide a much-needed alternative to the traditional four-year experience.

Stephanie Sy:

It expands the Pell Grant program, which first rolled out in 1973 to give students from low-income households a path to higher education and ideally a path into the middle class.

Pell Grants help fund college-style courses at least a semester or 15 weeks' long. Now, under Workforce Pell, short courses between eight to 15 weeks in length qualify.

Molly Dodge, Senior Vice President of Work Force and Careers, Ivy Tech Community College: Fifty-eight percent of our students access federal Pell.

Stephanie Sy:

Molly Dodge, Ivy Tech's senior vice president of work force and careers, has advocated for the change for more than a decade.

Molly Dodge:

In Indiana, we're a bit competitive, so we wanted to be first, but we were thrilled to have such a quick turnaround on the approval and the opportunity to now launch a Workforce Pell program.

Stephanie Sy:

To be eligible for funding, programs must train students for occupations defined by each state as high skill, high wage or in demand and meet federal requirements.

Molly Dodge:

Workforce Pell has what we call the 70/70 rule, meaning 70 percent of our learners need to complete the program, which has not been an issue at Ivy Tech, but also 70 percent of the cohort enrolled in a Workforce Pell pathway have to be employed associated with that training six months after they graduate.

Stephanie Sy:

The federal government started accepting applications in July. And so far, 21 programs across six states have been approved to train future emergency medical technicians, firefighters, electrical line workers, and more. Once Workforce Pell rolls out nationwide, an estimated 190,000 students per year will receive an average grant of $2,200.

Ivy Tech expects the funding to especially benefit its adult learners, many of whom, like CCMA students Kaitlynn Creason and Terra Randolph, are juggling parenting, work, and school.

Terra Randolph, Student, Ivy Tech Community College:

I really want to be a nurse, but having my two children and then being young, I just knew that getting my foot in the door would help me eventually make that goal.

Stephanie Sy:

They say being able to enter a medical occupation after only two months is a major bonus.

Kaitlynn Creason, Student, Ivy Tech Community College:

If I were doing a two-year program, it's like, dang, my kid's going to be 5 by the time I finally get one step closer. So I think that would be just a little bit discouraging.

Stephanie Sy:

What about you, Terra? Do you think that, without this, you would not have a path towards postsecondary education?

Terra Randolph:

To an extent, yes, because nowadays, with the economy, like, it's hard. It's hard to raise a family off of one person's income. And with it being a shortened course, it allows me to get out there quicker.

Stephanie Sy:

Some states identified this need years ago. Here in Indiana, the Workforce Ready Grants have existed since 2017, helping students fund those shorter-term vocational courses.

This year, demand for that state funding exceeded supply; 41-year-old father Jenkins Reese counts himself lucky. It covered his tuition for a three-week commercial driver's license.

Jenkins Reese, Graduate, Vincennes University:

I was ecstatic that I was able to get the grant to do it, so -- because this is going to help my family tremendously.

Stephanie Sy:

He owns a construction company, but with work scarce in the winter, truck driving will help support his family of eight.

Jenkins Reese:

Jobs are already coming in recruiting us to work for them. So I really don't even have to go look for the work. That's a great benefit of it.

Stephanie Sy:

According to Indiana, grant recipients who complete their training programs increase their salaries by about $6,800 a year. But skeptics say short-term courses may not all live up to their promise.

Wesley Whistle, New America:

I think some of these programs will have really great outcomes. I worry that more of them will not.

Stephanie Sy:

Wesley Whistle works on student success and affordability at New America, a progressive think tank where he's advised over 30 states on their rollout of Workforce Pell.

Wesley Whistle:

We have to do right by our Pell students, because, if we don't put in the right guardrails, then we really risk sending them into programs with taxpayer money that actually won't actually pay off for them.

Stephanie Sy:

He points to research suggesting that the earnings boost from short-term certificates is short-lived, and says they are no substitute for a college degree.

Wesley Whistle:

One of my biggest concerns with Workforce Pell over the last decade that I worked on this has been the risk of a potential -- quote, unquote -- "diversion effect," where when you're talking to a low-income student, when you tell them that they can go for eight weeks and get a middle-class job, that's really promising.

And the problem is, if that reality doesn't line up in many cases, right, all the evidence says the more education you get, on average, the more training you have, the higher earning potential you have.

Molly Dodge:

I think there's a both/and for accelerated programs, for associate degree programs, for four-year programs.

Stephanie Sy:

But back at Ivy Tech, Molly Dodge says a student can build on Workforce Pell programs.

Molly Dodge:

We need to offer as many pathways as possible for students to access the education that they need to qualify for a role.

Then we, the employers, postsecondary, need to work together to ensure those students then have access to upskilling pathways to continue their education.

Stephanie Sy:

Student Makaila Collins is already applying for certified clinical medical assistant roles, but her income might face at least a temporary hit.

Makaila Collins:

Even if it is a pay cut, it's worth it because I always tell people, I love waitressing, but I'm not passionate about it like I'm passionate about health care.

Stephanie Sy:

And she says worth it to get herself one step closer to becoming a full-fledged nurse.

Makaila Collins:

I can't wait for the day that I'm out of school and I can sit back and be like, wow, I really did that. Wow, I'm really proud of myself for doing that.

Stephanie Sy:

For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy in Anderson, Indiana.

title: New study signals rethink of overseas education among India’s Gen Z
summary:
Cost and visa concerns are tempering overseas ambitions, an Emeritus survey finds, as international programs in India appeal to students weighing where and how to pursue a global education.

The post New study signals rethink of overseas education among India’s Gen Z appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Among young Indians surveyed who would consider studying abroad, nearly half say their interest has declined over the past year, with rising costs and immigration uncertainty weighing on their plans as international universities offer alternatives closer to home.

Emeritus’s India Gen Z Outlook 2026: The No Cap Generation found that 71% of respondents were interested in overseas study, although 48% of that group said their interest had declined compared with a year earlier.

Among those reporting declining interest, 37% cited rising costs, 26% pointed to visa and immigration policies, and 24% identified safety and political uncertainty in other countries.

The reasons for considering overseas education remained largely career-focused, with 40% citing higher earning potential and 39% better job opportunities, followed by higher-quality content and knowledge, and stronger professional networks.

Ashwin Damera, co-founder and CEO of Emeritus, told The PIE News that students were reconsidering destinations, delaying plans or reassessing overseas study, with different patterns across life stages.

“They are citing rising visa uncertainties, geopolitical turbulence, and costs that are significantly impacting their choices,” he said.

For early-career respondents, he argued, the decision depended on timing and the expected return on their investment.

“They are already in the workforce and more likely to consider overseas study as a deliberate, planned future investment rather than an immediate choice.”

Conducted in March, the survey covered 1,010 Indians aged 15–28 across pre-college, undergraduate or postgraduate-transition, and early-career stages, capturing intentions rather than subsequent applications or enrolments.

Emeritus said respondents came from more than 50 cities, including Mumbai, Delhi, Bengaluru, Bhopal, Jaipur and Kochi, belonged to socioeconomic classifications A1, A2, A3 and B1, and were not recruited from its customers or learner base.

Alongside overseas interest, 68% of all respondents said they would be likely or extremely likely to pursue a program offered in India by an international university.

These (international university) campuses are not serving only students who were always going to stay, they are drawing in a broader audience than that

Ashwin Damera, Emeritus

Separately, 87% of pre-college respondents and 92% of the transitioning group expressed interest in studying in India within two years, figures Emeritus clarified referred to domestic study generally rather than specifically to international universities.

Respondents could consider both domestic and overseas options, while programs combining study in India with time abroad appealed to 39% of transitioning students and 27% of pre-college respondents.

For Emeritus, which supports several international universities’ India operations, including institutions from the UK and US, the findings point to a potential market beyond families already committed to domestic education.

In August, Damera described students at campuses the company supports as mostly people wanting to “study in India, live in India, work in India, build for India”, with undergraduate enrolments expected to dominate.

Asked whether the research changed that assessment, he said the campuses could serve both that group and students reconsidering overseas options.

“These campuses are not serving only students who were always going to stay, they are drawing in a broader audience than that,” he said.

Plans to return to India can also coexist with overseas study ambitions, with Oxford International’s separate mobility survey, reported by The PIE earlier this year, finding that 81% of surveyed study-abroad aspirants intended to return home after their courses.

The financial proposition also depends on which alternatives families are weighing, with international campuses offering savings against overseas study while charging substantial premiums within India.

Research by Rahul Choudaha, managing director of DrEducation Research, reported in August put average annual tuition at INR 13.3 lakh (approximately £10,500) for undergraduate programs and INR 17.2 lakh (approximately £13,600) for postgraduate programs across the campuses examined.

First-year undergraduate tuition at the India campuses averaged 115% more than at selected leading Indian private universities, but approximately 36% of the fees at their overseas parent campuses, before scholarships.

The comparison also excluded overseas living and travel costs, which Damera argued were central to how families assessed the India option.

“A student going abroad is not just paying tuition, they are paying for visa fees, travel, accommodation, and years of living costs in a foreign country,” he said.

He also highlighted merit- and need-based scholarships, arguing that universities were seeking to broaden access while maintaining their academic expectations.

Damera said Emeritus was working with the Maharashtra chief minister’s office and the University of Bristol to offer full scholarships to selected students from rural government schools in the state.

“They will not lower their standards, but they also understand that cost should not become a barrier to talent.”

The findings show interest in these programs, but do not establish what students would be willing or able to pay for them.

Confidence in the model also rests on what happens after graduation, with surveys covered by The PIE in May finding that more than 70% of employers prioritised workplace readiness over institutional reputation.

Among schools surveyed, 48% considered it too early to confidently recommend international branch campuses, highlighting the distance between awareness of a university’s name and confidence in its local provision.

Some employment evidence was already emerging: Deakin reported in March that around 50–60% of its GIFT City students had secured jobs, while others were completing internships and work-integrated learning.

For newer campuses, the record remains less developed, with Damera previously describing the initial recruitment cycle as “year zero” because late approvals had left institutions little time to recruit.

Damera pointed to corporate partnerships, campus locations near industry and career services as ways of preparing students for employment, while arguing that international education’s appeal extended beyond the qualification itself.

“Intellectual capital: who is teaching you and what is the quality of what you are being taught. Brand capital: when you walk into a room of recruiters, does the name behind your degree speak before you do. And social capital: the peer network you build alongside people who will go on to lead, build, and create,” he said.

title: Leading With Your Heart and Guarding It Too: Lessons on Sustainability from Fifteen Years of School Leadership
summary:
Leadership Begins with the Heart For 15 years, I tried to be the kind of school leader I would have wanted, which was one who met everyone’s needs all the time. I believed leadership begins with kindness. I believed it was essential to truly know people and to show up for them in a sincere, […]

The post Leading With Your Heart and Guarding It Too: Lessons on Sustainability from Fifteen Years of School Leadership appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Leadership Begins with the Heart

For 15 years, I tried to be the kind of school leader I would have wanted, which was one who met everyone’s needs all the time. I believed leadership begins with kindness. I believed it was essential to truly know people and to show up for them in a sincere, authentic way. I believed that if you gave your whole heart to a community, they would feel cared for and, in turn, do their best work for students and for one another, and with this leadership style in place, they did. I received positive feedback on a daily basis and I knew I was onto something. What I did not understand at the time was this: an open heart without boundaries slowly becomes an unsustainable one.

Naming a Philosophy of Care

In 2022, Rowman & Littlefield published The Heart of School Leadership (Stahl, 2022), a book I wrote based on my 15 years as a teacher and 15 years as school leader. In it, I organized my philosophy into 50 areas I believed were essential to effective leadership ranging from kindness and visibility to instructional leadership and equity. These areas were supported by research, specifically the Challenge to Care (Noddings, 2005), among others.

My book grew out of a deeply meaningful year when I served as a substitute principal in a large public elementary school. When that year ended, the faculty and staff gave me a red leather journal with a heart embossed on the front, filled with handwritten notes. It was more valuable than any title or salary I had earned. Those notes helped me unlock what I believed mattered most in leadership, and these ideals became the basis for my leadership book. This one was included in my preface:

‘Don’t cry because she is gone, smile because she was here.’ I heard this quote at a memorial service yesterday for a woman who died just nine days’ shy of her 101st birthday. She was described as an angel on earth—sweet, subdued, and endlessly patient. I knew her well–it was an apt description. Yet, when those words were spoken, it was you who sprang to mind. At one time or another, I have worked in every school, both public and private, in this district. Over the years, I have worked with more administrators than I can count. Happily, I have been able to work with all of them. So when you came to our school, I expected the experience to be the same. It was. Here is what I didn’t expect. I didn’t expect to find a person behind the desk who treated everyone equally, whose warmth was real, and whose joy was freely expressed and meant for all.’

After leaving school leadership to teach college full time, I began using my book in my graduate courses. At the end of each semester, I asked students to select three leadership areas and reflect on how they would influence their future practice. The discussions were powerful. This assignment also led to discussions about school culture, teaching philosophy, leadership style, and the effect of kindness and positivity in schools. Students affirmed the importance of relationships, positivity, visibility, and trust. I also believed I had modeled what I had written and the students confirmed this. Then something shifted.

When Students Redefined Care

When I presented my leadership framework at a professional conference, educators affirmed many of the relational traits I described. But they also raised questions I had not anticipated. Curious, I later sought IRB approval to more formally gather feedback from my graduate students. They weren’t yet working as teachers or leaders in the field so I was curious to see what they thought. It was an extra credit assignment where they rated the 50 categories as “important,” “somewhat important” or “not important” and added specific comments where they had feedback.

Similar to the conference attendees, the graduate students supported relational leadership, but not leadership that meant being everything to everyone. They spoke about sustainability. About balance. About protecting personal health and family life. They did not reject care-based leadership. They redefined it. Their feedback unsettled me on several levels and made me wonder if I had possibly modeled and written about unsustainable leadership?

When Devotion Becomes Depletion

For years, I had worn constant availability as a badge of honor. I answered calls while on vacation. I remember standing in Times Square, phone to my ear, listening to a teachers’ issue during spring break because it felt like what a committed leader would do, and I sincerely wanted to help. It’s who I am at my core. I was constantly available and responsive. I knew teachers’ children and dogs by name, and kept in touch with many after I left my last position. I attended every possible event. I was professionally available and often emotionally available, serving as part counselor as well as administrator. I believed this was devotion. In hindsight, I can see now that I had mistaken depletion for dedication.

There was also another layer to confront. I had worked alongside male leaders who practiced leadership differently and were far less visible and available than I was. Whether because of gendered expectations or my own internal standards, the responsibility to be endlessly visible and accessible fell primarily on me. It was fulfilling. It was meaningful. But in hindsight, it was also heavy.

Transition or Recovery?

When I transitioned into higher education, I experienced an quiet, unexpected loss of identity. I was no longer needed in the same urgent way. No one was calling during crises. No one required immediate decisions that only I could make. The teaching part came naturally, but I had also entered a world focused on research, publishing, and long-term scholarly contribution. It took me a while to understand this and I told myself I was simply in transition. It took some time to realize I was actually in recovery.

Over the next several years, I was offered multiple leadership positions and encouraged to return to school leadership. Each time, I felt a visceral resistance I could not fully explain. I had loved serving as a school leader and during my tenure I was honestly happy and energized. I am also someone who regularly follows directions and does what I am told, so in many ways as a leader I was responding to what people asked of me and needed, and above all following, “the Golden Rule.” After being away from leadership for a few years, something in me knew I could not return to that version of myself, and the graduate students’ feedback helped me understand why.

Sustainable Leadership for the Next Generation

Care-based leadership is essential. Schools are human institutions, and relationships matter deeply. But care that consumes the caregiver eventually undermines itself. Sustainable leadership requires boundaries, not as a retreat from responsibility, but as a protection of it. I still believe leadership begins with the heart. I still believe in knowing people, showing up, and building cultures of kindness, and I honestly wouldn’t change anything about my 15 years as a school leader because I am proud I gave so much. I believe I created a positive school culture. I now understand that I couldn’t have continued in that way, and that kindness must extend inward as well.

As I reflected on my last few years in higher education, I saw that I had begun replicating the same pattern with my college students and have been committed to constant responsiveness, extreme care and immediate availability. I think I did not recognize the toll it was beginning to take until I reviewed the responses from my study. I think that maybe I was looking for the same validation, and my student feedback conveyed I was giving my all, but if that were true, what was I actually teaching them as future educators?

The most meaningful lesson about leadership did not come from my years in administration or my own reflection after leaving it. It came from the graduate students who challenged my definition of care. They taught me that being everything to everyone is not the highest form of leadership. Sustainability is. To lead with your heart, you must also protect it.

Dr. Mary Louise Stahl is currently an Assistant Professor at Niagara University in New York and also an adjunct professor at the State University of New York at Fredonia. She earned her PhD in Educational Leadership in 2016 from the State University of New York at Buffalo, with her dissertation, “Chinese Students in United States High Schools.” She has worked for over 30 years in education, as a teacher, a school leader, a college professor and a writer. In 2022 Rowman & Littlefield published her book, the Heart of School Leadership.

References

Noddings, N. (2005). The challenge to care: An alternative approach to education. New York: Teachers College Press.

Stahl, M.L. (2002). The heart of school leadership. Rowman & Littlefield.

title: How Institutions Are Adopting a Human-Centered Approach to IT
summary:
As colleges and universities adopt new technology, the most consequential question may be how they support the people expected to use it. A number of issues on the 2027 EDUCAUSE Top 10 list emphasize the need to integrate humanity into technology experiences. 
Mark McCormack, interim vice president of research, insights and analytics for EDUCAUSE, summed it up: “I think issue No. 5 [designing human-centric technology experiences] is the clearest and boldest declaration of the value of designing our systems, tools and technology experiences with the human person in mind, with what they…
full_text:
Security Awareness Training Improves Cyber Vigilance

IT security teams are staying in closer contact with the campus community, McCormack said.

“Our cybersecurity teams and leaders are increasingly sensitive to the needs of the individual,” he said. “What work are they trying to get done? What is the student trying to accomplish? How can we factor that into how we design and support our security needs so that we're not just viewed as a barrier? We're helping to enable their work in a safe way.”

The EDUCAUSE Top 10 emphasizes the need to balance strong cybersecurity measures with autonomy and trust of the individual. Institutions are doing what they can to protect student and institutional data via technology and security strategies, but they’re also realizing the value of making sure the campus community stays vigilant against cyberthreats. Cybersecurity awareness training is a key element of this strategy.

At Washington University in St. Louis, the cybersecurity team is trying to move beyond training as a compliance exercise.

“We serve more than 40,000 brilliant scholars, physicians, students and staff working at the frontiers of discovery, and they carry an enormous cognitive load,” said Quint Smith, director of the Information Security Awareness, Behavior and Culture (ABC) Program. “We treat them as capable, extremely busy partners in protecting the systems and data that drive innovation at our institution.”

The team’s approach includes tailored messaging, hands-on activities and training timed to the academic and clinical calendar. The team found data showing that annual training does not meaningfully reduce phishing attacks.

READ MORE: Building cyber resilience around risk protects institutions.

“Cognitive load theory reminds us that working memory is limited, people do not like passive, repetitive content like once-a-year training videos,” said Christina Pomianek-Smith, information security analyst at WashU. “Instead of building a security mindset, we may be unintentionally training people to ignore us.”

The team conducted a study comparing traditional hourlong cybersecurity training sessions with microlearning modules delivered at different intervals. Early data from the study has shown that participants prefer monthly training and that those who received monthly training were less likely to open or click through phishing simulation emails. Monthly training also had the highest compliance rate, at around 75%.

“Our monthly group included the most people streaming, had the lowest click rate of simulated phishing, and rated their experience the highest,” Smith said. “We also saw microlearning participants use the phishing alert button. The ABC program is moving all participants to a monthly model. We chose the one people prefer, and that that keeps security in front of them most often.”

DISCOVER: Quantifying cyber risk can help justify technology investments.

IT Support Teams Build Trust With End Users

At Yale University, the human-centered approach starts with recognizing that faculty are not a single kind of IT user. Higher education institutions are full of diverse users with a range of needs and comfort levels. A humanities professor and a chemistry professor might have completely different relationships to technology. Yale’s frontline support team recognizes this and is organized around discipline zones, tailoring its offerings accordingly.

“Our role is to translate complex systems into practical solutions that people can rely on in their daily work,” said Rachel Feinmesser, associate director of IT. “That requires more than just technical knowledge; it requires listening, empathy and an understanding of what people are actually trying to accomplish.”

That distinction changes how support staff respond. In one example Feinmesser shared, a faculty member’s trouble accessing files could have prompted a quick link to instructions. Instead, a technician investigated the person’s actual workflow, learned that files were spread across devices and storage locations, and developed visual cues to help. The ticket stayed open for 28 days — not because the team was slow, but because the client needed time to test whether the solution worked.

LEARN MORE: Year-round learning requires always-on support.

Feinmesser also described IT as a partner in keeping research moving. In one case, a lab facing high data storage costs wanted to use a personal storage server. The support team coordinated with networking and information security to assess whether the approach would fit Yale’s systems, then helped migrate the data.

“When we understand the people behind the problems, we don’t just resolve the tickets; we strengthen the research community itself,” she said.

Feinmesser described frontline support’s role as acting like a concierge, connecting users to the people and resources on campus that can help them meet their goals. Communication is an integral part of that service, not an extra step.

“Communication is often the key to saving any interaction, even if what you have to convey is bad news,” she said.

IT staff should meet users at their level of technical knowledge, Feinmesser said. Don’t use technical jargon that will go over their heads, but don’t talk down to those who have technical backgrounds. Keep clients informed when work is delayed, and close the loop rather than assuming a fix is complete. The goal, she said, is to leave people with understanding, confidence and trust.

Click the banner below to subscribe to our weekly newsletter.

Responsible AI Adoption Requires Human Agency

Technology leaders are increasingly seeing the value of keeping humans in the loop when it comes to AI adoption. University of Michigan CIO Ravi Pendse described responsible AI as an ongoing practice, not a one-time policy decision, and said institutions should be deliberate about AI use.

“The human has to be the center of what we do,” Pendse said. “We need to know when to use AI and when not to use AI, and make sure that humans review any consequential decisions. Human judgment has to be always in the center.”

Keeping humans at the center also means preserving human agency in everyday use. Pendse cautioned against reflexively turning to an AI tool for every task. He encouraged people to consider their own thoughts first and use AI intentionally rather than letting it replace their own thinking.

UP NEXT: Build an AI strategy around your institution’s goals.

The University of Michigan’s broader AI strategy reflects the same emphasis on human control, Pendse said. He described an ecosystem of tools, including a codeless platform called Maizey, and an AI app store built around connectors to institutional services, called M-Connectors. These tools are intended to help the university community solve practical problems and reduce repetitive work.

But Pendse stressed that automation should not mean handing over unrestricted authority.

“The idea of M-Connectors is they bring the right information together, but people are still vital to what comes next,” Pendse said. “At no point have we deployed these agents to say, ‘Delete all my emails.’ Human agency must always be in the center of it. Approval is always needed.”

Ultimately AI’s impact will depend on the choices people make, Pendse said. That requires continuous learning, open discussion and space for a range of voices and opinions.

As AI and other technologies advance, higher ed IT leaders are incorporating human-centric principles into a variety of technological areas, which McCormack said is part of the current era of change higher ed finds itself in.

“They’re adapting with purpose,” he said. “They’re staying anchored to what they value and what their goals and mission are as an institution, and they’re adapting with people at the center of it.”

title: Community engagement in higher education: is its moment finally arriving?
summary: by Thomas Farnell Community engagement has long occupied a curious position in higher education. Universities have been expected to contribute to society beyond teaching and research, and community engagement has existed in practice for decades. Yet it has often remained … Continue reading →
full_text:
by Thomas Farnell

Community engagement has long occupied a curious position in higher education. Universities have been expected to contribute to society beyond teaching and research, and community engagement has existed in practice for decades. Yet it has often remained fragmented, unevenly recognised and peripheral to the policies and structures that shape what universities do.

Is this now changing? There are signs that it may be. In 2026, UNESCO became the first intergovernmental organisation to specifically name “community engagement” as one of the three missions of higher education, alongside research and teaching. At the same time, universities, European University alliances, networks and national initiatives are increasingly treating engagement not simply as a collection of activities, but as part of the core identity and mission of higher education.

An old idea, narrowed over time

Community engagement in higher education can be understood as how universities address societal needs in partnership with external communities, with “communities” encompassing public authorities, businesses, schools, civil society and citizens. The underlying idea is far from new. From their origins, universities have been fundamentally societal institutions, shaped by and responsive to external needs.

The emergence of the “third mission” in the late twentieth century reinforced the idea that universities contribute to society beyond teaching and research. However, over time, this broader societal role was increasingly subsumed under an economic narrative. The third mission came to be interpreted largely in terms of knowledge transfer, commercialisation and contribution to the knowledge economy. Economic and technological contributions took precedence over broader social and civic dimensions.

The issue, therefore, has never been the absence of engagement. Rather, community engagement has often existed without being clearly named, connected or supported as a coherent mission.

Europe’s “fourth mission”: promising, but weakly operationalised

For a period, European policy appeared to offer a possible way forward. In 2017, the European Commission referred to “civic universities” in its Renewed Agenda for Higher Education. In 2020, its vision for the European Education Area went further by introducing “service to society” as a fourth mission of higher education, complementing teaching, research and innovation and together forming a “knowledge square”.

In theory, this was promising. Distinguishing a mission focused on service to society from innovation could have created clearer space for universities’ broader social and civic role. The European Universities Initiative also seemed well placed to operationalise this ambition. Yet the results have been ambiguous. While reports on the activities on European university alliances show that community engagement initiatives are widespread across European University alliances, “service to society” has not acquired the weight one might expect from a genuine fourth mission. It is remains nested within broader agendas of innovation, society and economy, regional development or the green and digital transitions.

The problem, therefore, is not the absence of recognition of universities’ societal role, but the gap between broad mission-level ambition and narrower operationalisation.

Practice is beginning to move ahead of policy

On the ground, however, something more interesting is happening. Community engagement is not only expanding as an activity; in some cases it is being treated as a defining feature of university identity and as a strategic orientation that is acquiring institutional form.

Three European University alliances illustrate this broader move:

The EMERGE alliance offers perhaps the most explicit conceptual repositioning: rather than treating societal engagement as a consequence of teaching and research, it describes it as its “first mission”.

The EUNICoast alliance is embedding community engagement as an area of institutional development requiring evidence, reflection, planning and follow-up, including institutional reporting and action plans for all member institutions.

The YUFE alliance, meanwhile, positions community engagement as a transversal principle integrated across the alliance’s activities through its Community Engagement Declaration 2025–2030.

In these cases, community engagement is moving from something universities do towards something that helps define what universities are.

A recognisable field is emerging

These developments are supported by a wider transnational movement. Community engagement is increasingly acquiring the features of a recognisable field: shared concepts, methods, tools, platforms, networks, institutional examples and policy advocates. The TEFCE Toolbox provided one of the first structured European frameworks for institutional self-reflection on community engagement. Since then, further resources for action planning, university-community partnerships and community-engaged curricula have been developed and gathered through the platform www.community-engagement.eu. European networks support service-learning and community-based research, while bodies such as the Talloires Network of Engaged Universities and the UNESCO Chair in Community-Based Research and Social Responsibility in Higher Education connect this agenda globally.

National and regional developments point in a similar direction, although unevenly. Flanders and Catalonia have substantial engagement activity but still fragmented policy frameworks. Ireland has gone further in recognising engagement alongside teaching and research and developing national support infrastructure for engagement. In the United Kingdom, the recent civic university agenda has provided new impetus for universities and communities to define shared place-based commitments.

So “practice ahead of policy” is important, but incomplete. In some systems, policy is beginning to catch up.

The time is now

If ever there was a time for universities to demonstrate their capacity to work proactively with communities in addressing complex societal challenges, it is now. And many universities are already acting. The challenge for policy is no longer simply to encourage isolated examples of good practice. It is to recognise and support the emerging infrastructure through which community engagement can become a coherent and sustainable mission of higher education.

Ultimately, the challenge is not to introduce something entirely new, but to name, define, connect and strengthen what already exists. Whether community engagement is called a third, fourth or even first mission matters less than whether it is recognised as a core mission and supported accordingly. Universities are moving. Policy now needs to catch up.

This blog is adapted from the author’s article in Policy Reviews in Higher Education: Farnell, T (2026) Community engagement in higher education: from fragmented practice to core mission?

title: AI Literacy im Studium: Hochschulen und Studierende in der Pflicht
summary:
Wie steht es eigentlich um die AI Literacy von Studierenden? Roksana Rybicka, Katharina Westphal und Janis Jaspers, die dieses Jahr DigitalChangeMaker am HFD sind, setzen sich mit der Frage im Thementrack „Shaping AI“ auseinander. In diesem Blogbeitrag erklären sie, warum man AI Literacy nicht an der Frequenz der KI-Nutzung messen kann. Außerdem diskutieren, sie, wie Hochschulen mehr zu Orten gemacht werden können, an denen gemeinsam ausgehandelt und erprobt werden kann, was Lernen mit generativer KI bedeutet.

The post AI Literacy im Studium: Hochschulen und Studierende in der Pflicht appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
„Darf ich die KI dafür überhaupt verwenden?“ Diese Frage begegnet Studierenden inzwischen in vielfältigen Situationen des Studienalltags. Manche nutzen KI selbstverständlich für Recherche, Schreiben oder Prüfungsvorbereitung. Andere verzichten darauf, weil sie nicht wissen, was erlaubt ist. Wieder andere nutzen KI, sind sich aber unsicher, wie zuverlässig die Ergebnisse sind oder an welcher Stelle Unterstützung in die Übernahme eigener Leistungen übergeht.

Diese unterschiedlichen Erfahrungen zeigen: KI ist im Studium angekommen. Wie kompetent Studierende damit umgehen können, ist damit jedoch noch nicht beantwortet – und die Gründe für eine nicht kompetente Nutzung können vielfältig sein: mangelnde Erfahrung im kritischen Umgang mit KI-generierten Inhalten, fehlende methodische Werkzeuge oder schlicht unzureichende Vorbereitung im Studium (Bosse et al., 2026 und Rockstroh, 2025).

Ausgangspunkt dieses Beitrags sind Erfahrungen und Diskussionen aus unserer Arbeit im studentischen Shaping AI Track der DigitalChangeMaker-Initiative. Wir beschäftigen uns deshalb mit der Frage, was studentische Erfahrungen über den aktuellen Stand von AI Literacy an Hochschulen zeigen.

Dabei interessiert uns weniger, welche Tools Studierende verwenden, sondern welche Kompetenzen, Unsicherheiten und Unterstützungsbedarfe im Studienalltag sichtbar werden und welche Rolle Hochschulen bei deren Entwicklung spielen. Denn wenn Studierende lernen sollen, KI kritisch, reflektiert und verantwortungsvoll einzusetzen, stellt sich auch die Frage: Wo und wie lernen sie das eigentlich?

Eine studierende Person sitzt an einer Hausarbeit und möchte zunächst nur ihre Gliederung überprüfen. Sie gibt ihre ersten Ideen in ein KI-Tool ein und erhält innerhalb weniger Sekunden mehrere alternative Strukturen und Argumentationslinien. Einige Vorschläge helfen ihr weiter, andere passen nicht zu ihrer Fragestellung. Eine vorgeschlagene Quelle klingt überzeugend, lässt sich bei genauerer Suche jedoch nicht finden. Die studierende Person verwirft die Quelle und arbeitet weiter. Hat sie KI kompetent genutzt?

Eine andere Person verwendet KI bereits selbstverständlich. Sie lässt sich schwierige Konzepte erklären, entwickelt Ideen mit einem Sprachmodell und überarbeitet anschließend ihre Texte. Die technische Nutzung fällt ihr leicht. Schwieriger wird die Frage, wo Unterstützung aufhört und die eigene Leistung beginnt. Wenn das Sprachmodell bereits Argumente, Gegenargumente und eine mögliche Struktur entwickelt, welche Leistung soll dann noch selbst erbracht werden?

Daneben gibt es Studierende, die KI kaum nutzen. Sie lehnen es nicht unbedingt aus grundsätzlicher Ablehnung ab, sondern weil sie nicht wissen, was in ihrem Studiengang, in einer bestimmten Lehrveranstaltung oder in einer Prüfung erlaubt ist. Die Nichtnutzung ist in diesem Fall nicht unbedingt eine bewusste Entscheidung gegen KI. Sie kann auch Ausdruck fehlender Orientierung sein.

Drei Situationen, drei unterschiedliche Ausgangslagen und vier Fragen, die sich durch den Studienalltag ziehen: Was darf ich? Was kann ich? Was sollte ich? Und vor allem: Was muss ich selbst können?

Genau an solchen Entscheidungen wird AI Literacy sichtbar. Dazu gehören zweifellos anwendungsbezogene Fähigkeiten: geeignete Tools auswählen, Prompts formulieren, Ergebnisse überprüfen und KI sinnvoll einsetzen. AI Literacy reicht jedoch darüber hinaus. Sie umfasst auch die Fähigkeit, KI-Systeme und ihre Ergebnisse kritisch einzuschätzen, Nutzungskontexte zu beurteilen und zu reflektieren, welche Aufgaben sinnvoll delegiert werden können – und welche nicht.

Der UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Students beschreibt zwölf Kompetenzen in vier Dimensionen: einen menschenzentrierten Umgang mit KI, die Ethik von KI, KI-Techniken und -Anwendungen sowie das Design von KI-Systemen. Die Kompetenzen werden über die Entwicklungsstufen „Understand“, „Apply“ und „Create“ strukturiert (Miao et al., 2024). Das Framework richtet sich nicht spezifisch an Hochschulen. Es macht jedoch deutlich, dass AI Literacy nicht mit der Fähigkeit gleichgesetzt werden kann, ein KI-Tool technisch zu bedienen.

Auch der KI-Kompetenzrahmen Hochschule des Digital Lehre Hub Niedersachsen greift diese Mehrdimensionalität für den Hochschulbereich auf. Neben technologischen Grundlagen werden rechtliche und ethische Rahmenbedingungen, Anwendung und Reflexion berücksichtigt (Digital Lehre Hub Niedersachsen, 2026).

Beide Ansätze machen deutlich: AI Literacy verbindet Wissen über KI mit Anwendung, Bewertung und Reflexion. Für den Hochschulalltag stellt sich jedoch eine weitere Frage: Wie werden solche abstrakten Kompetenzen in konkreten Lern- und Entscheidungssituationen wirksam?

Eine studierende Person begegnet im Studienalltag nicht der abstrakten Kompetenz „kritische Bewertung von KI“. Eine studierende Person beschäftigt sich nicht theoretisch mit „Human Agency“. Sie muss entscheiden, ob sie die Argumentation für ihre Hausarbeit selbst entwickelt oder diese Aufgabe an ein Sprachmodell delegiert. Und eine Lehrperson steht nicht vor der Kategorie „ethische Reflexion“, sondern vor der konkreten Frage, wie mit KI-Nutzung in einer Prüfungsleistung umgegangen werden soll.

Die eingangs beschriebenen Situationen zeigen unterschiedliche Lern- und Unterstützungsbedarfe. Wer KI bereits routiniert nutzt, benötigt möglicherweise weniger Unterstützung bei der technischen Anwendung als Gelegenheiten zur Reflexion. Wer KI nutzen möchte, aber nicht weiß wie, braucht anwendungsbezogenes Wissen und Möglichkeiten zum Erproben. Und wer aufgrund unklarer Regeln auf KI verzichtet, benötigt zunächst Orientierung. AI Literacy beginnt deshalb nicht für alle Studierenden am selben Punkt.

Damit wird deutlich: Intensive KI-Nutzung ist nicht automatisch Ausdruck hoher AI Literacy. Umgekehrt bedeutet geringe Nutzung nicht zwangsläufig, dass AI Literacy fehlt. Zur kompetenten Auseinandersetzung mit KI gehört möglicherweise auch die Fähigkeit, begründet auf ihren Einsatz zu verzichten.

Was zunächst wie eine individuelle Kompetenzfrage erscheint, ist deshalb immer auch eine Frage institutioneller Bedingungen.

Fragt eine studierende Person, ob sie ChatGPT für ihre Hausarbeit verwenden darf, fehlt nicht unbedingt Wissen über das Tool, sondern möglicherweise institutionelle Orientierung. Weiß eine studierende Person zwar, dass KI-Ausgaben überprüft werden müssen, hat aber nie gelernt, wie eine solche Überprüfung konkret funktioniert, fehlt eine Lerngelegenheit. Und bleibt unklar, welche KI-Nutzung mit einer Prüfungsleistung vereinbar ist, betrifft das nicht nur die Kompetenz der Studierenden, sondern ebenso die Gestaltung der Prüfung.

Die Frage „Darf ich KI verwenden?“ reicht deshalb häufig nicht aus. Interessanter ist die Frage: Welche Rolle kann KI in diesem konkreten Lernprozess übernehmen, ohne das eigentliche Lernziel zu ersetzen? Damit verschiebt sich die Perspektive von der individuellen Nutzung zur Gestaltung von Lehre und Studium.

Kompetenzrahmen bieten dafür wichtige Orientierung: Sie benennen, welche Fähigkeiten relevant sind. Noch nicht beantwortet ist damit jedoch, wie diese Fähigkeiten entstehen. Zwischen der Kompetenzbeschreibung „kritische Bewertung“ und der Entscheidung, ob eine KI-generierte Quelle vertrauenswürdig ist, liegt ein Lernprozess. Hochschulen müssen deshalb nicht nur beschreiben, was Studierende können sollen, sondern auch Lerngelegenheiten schaffen, in denen diese Fähigkeiten erprobt und reflektiert werden können.

Dass diese Fragen längst Teil des Hochschulalltags sind, zeigen auch empirische Untersuchungen. Wie eine solche institutionelle Übersetzung aussehen kann, zeigt exemplarisch der Leuphana AI Campus. Dort wird AI Literacy in eine hochschulweite Lernarchitektur eingebettet. Neben unterschiedlichen Lernangeboten ist mit dem AI Literacy Hub auch ein Raum für Austausch, Erprobung und Reflexion vorgesehen. Interessant ist daran vor allem die Perspektive auf AI Literacy. Sie wird nicht allein als etwas verstanden, das Studierende individuell erwerben müssen. Vielmehr werden Räume geschaffen, in denen Kompetenz entstehen und gemeinsam entwickelt werden kann. Solche hochschulweiten Angebote können vor allem fächerübergreifende Grundlagen vermitteln: etwa Wissen über Funktionsweisen und Grenzen generativer KI, die kritische Prüfung von Ergebnissen sowie rechtliche und ethische Fragen der Nutzung.

Diese allgemeinen Kompetenzen müssen jedoch durch eine fachspezifische AI Literacy ergänzt werden. Denn ob und wie KI sinnvoll eingesetzt werden kann, hängt auch von den Methoden, Qualitätsmaßstäben und Erkenntnisweisen des jeweiligen Fachs ab. Was beispielsweise als wissenschaftlich belastbarer Nachweis, zulässige Unterstützung oder eigenständige Leistung gilt, lässt sich nicht immer fachübergreifend beantworten.

Gerade hier wird die studentische Perspektive relevant. Studierende erleben unmittelbar, dass der Umgang mit KI innerhalb einer Hochschule unterschiedlich geregelt und gelebt wird: In einer Lehrveranstaltung wird KI selbstverständlich eingesetzt, in einer anderen ist sie unerwünscht. Eine Lehrperson erwartet Transparenz, ohne genauer zu definieren, was dokumentiert werden soll. Ein Tool hilft beim Verständnis eines schwierigen Themas, während gleichzeitig unklar bleibt, ob es in einer Prüfungsleistung eingesetzt werden darf. Solche Situationen sind mehr als individuelle Irritationen. Sie können Hinweise darauf geben, wo sich Lernpraktiken bereits verändern, während institutionelle Regeln und Lehrpraktiken noch nicht überall Schritt halten.
